Article Title: War of NH blockades in Manipur: Kuki women body moves Supreme Court
Article Text:
CJI Kant said the blockade war must stop, groups must sit together, abjure violence, and cooperate with each other so that the supply of essential commodities and medicines are not disrupted.

NEW DELHI: Blockading NHs in Manipur by ethnic groups to inconvenience opponents is common but the Supreme Court on Friday took serious note of the humanitarian crisis such actions unleash after an NGO of Kuki women claimed that blockading of NH-2 and connected supply routes to Kangpokpi has left the population in there without food and healthcare.Senior advocate Anand Grover, appearing for Kuki Women Organisation for Human Rights, told a bench of CJI Surya Kant, and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that the NH-2 and supply routes to Kangpokpi has been blocked by Naga groups creating a crisis for the population and requested the SC to direct the Centre and the state to reopen the NH. “The state just can’t sit and do nothing,” he complained.Intervening in the matter, an Imphal-based NGO – International Meitei Organization – through senior advocate Ngangom Junior Luwang said the Kukis had been “responsible for blocking all major NHs in Manipur since May 2023, after the Kuki-Meitei ethnic clashes began, and now they are playing the ‘victim card' when faced with the consequences of such blockades by another ethnic group.”“It is a matter of record that since May 3, 2023, members of the community, of which the petitioner is a part of, have been blocking all major NHs in Manipur - NH2 (Imphal to Dimapur), NH-37 (Imphal to Silchar), and NH-102 (Imphal to Moreh) and except for intermittent flow of goods vehicles through extortion rackets reportedly perpetuated by Kuki community,” the NGO alleged.CJI Kant said the blockade war must stop, groups must sit together, abjure violence, and cooperate with each other so that the supply of essential commodities and medicines are not disrupted.When Luwang welcomed the CJI’s suggestion, Grover immediately offered the petitioner organisation’s cooperation but wondered who would bring the Naga group to the talks.SC issued notices to the Centre, Manipur govt and National Highway Authority of India (NHAI) and said the larger public interest demands removal of blockade of all NHs in the state as well as restoration of supply to Kangpokpi district.It said Grover assured that his client in cooperation with social organisations would work towards the same and recorded similar sentiments expressed by Luwang on behalf of the Meitei NGO. It asked all the parties to suggest modalities for reopening all NHS without engaging in blame games. It posted the matter for further hearing after two weeks.
Article Summary: CJI Surya Kant said the blockade war must stop, groups must sit together, abjure violence, and cooperate with each other. An NGO of Kuki women claimed that blockading of NH-2 and connected supply routes to Kangpokpi has left the population without food and healthcare.

NEW DELHI: Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal on Friday said she was “deeply touched” by Prime Minister Narendra Modi ’s “kind gesture” of reaching out to enquire about the health of her husband and party chief, Sukhbir Singh Badal , who was attacked at a gurdwara in Maharashtra’s Nanded a day earlier.This marked the Badal family's first reaction to the attack on the former Punjab deputy chief minister."Truly grateful, Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri @narendramodi ji, for your personal call to inquire about Sardar Sukhbir Singh Badal ji’s health and for your good wishes for his speedy recovery following the dastardly attack on him inside a Gurudwara Sahib in Nanded, Maharashtra," Harsimrat Badal, SAD's only Lok Sabha MP, wrote on X.She also thanked the prime minister for taking immediate cognisance of the incident and directing central investigating agencies to coordinate with the state police in the probe."Your concern, support and wishes during this difficult time mean a lot to all of us in the family, our party and to the people of Punjab. I am deeply touched by your kind gesture. I am also grateful to you for taking immediate cognisance of the incident and directing central investigating agencies to coordinate with Maharashtra Police in the probe," the Bathinda MP added.On Thursday, Sukhbir Singh Badal was injured after being attacked by a kirpan-wielding assailant while leaving the Mata Sahib Devaji Gurdwara at Mudkhed in Maharashtra’s Nanded district. The assailant was arrested at the spot.Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis ordered an inquiry into the attack and spoke to Sukhbir Singh Badal over the phone. The SAD president is learnt to have told Fadnavis that he was stable, ANI reported.Earlier, Badal was also targeted in an attempted shooting at the Golden Temple in Amritsar in December 2024 while he was performing “seva”. The attacker allegedly tried to fire at him but was overpowered before he could cause any harm.The 2024 attack took place while Badal was carrying out “seva” after the Akal Takht, the highest temporal authority in Sikhism, declared him a “tankhaiya,” or guilty of religious misconduct, over decisions taken by the SAD-led Punjab government between 2007 and 2017.The SAD and BJP, which currently lead the governments at the Centre and in Maharashtra, are former allies. In 2020, the SAD ended its alliance with the BJP in protest against the Centre’s contentious farm laws, which were later withdrawn.Sukhbir Singh Badal met Prime Minister Narendra Modi last week, triggering speculation that the former allies could reunite ahead of the Punjab assembly elections early next year.
Article Summary: Harsimrat Kaur Badal said she was “deeply touched” by Prime Minister Narendra Modi ’s “kind gesture” of reaching out to enquire about the health of her husband and party chief. Sukhbir Singh Badal was attacked at a gurdwara in Maharashtra’s Nanded a day earlier.

Article Title: In response to Pak PM Sharif, J&K CM Omar says IWT sucked ‘our blood’, calls for its cancellation
Article Text:
India placed the treaty in abeyance last year following the Pahalgam terror attack

SRINAGAR: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif warned at an event in Islamabad on Friday that Pakistan would take any step to protect its water rights under the Indus Waters Treaty , saying “every single drop” of Pakistan’s water is a “red line” and “India must come to the right path” or it would “be given a direct response”. His comments drew a reaction from Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah who said the treaty has been kept in abeyance and should remain so.“Yes, our blood. We have been saying this only, that our blood has been sucked. Thankfully Shehbaz Sharif came to his senses. This (IWT) has sucked the blood out of us. These are our rivers. We have the first right on them,” Omar told reporters here. “For the sake of saying, Pakistanis say that they are great sympathisers of Kashmiris. But when it comes to water, their sympathy disappears. Where was his sympathy when our permission to use our rivers was taken away from us,” the CM said.“Out of the six rivers, three which belonged to Punjab were kept by India and our three rivers were handed over to Pakistan. From then till today we are suffering the consequences of this Indus Waters Treaty,” Omar said, adding that under the treaty J&K could neither extract drinking water from the Chenab nor use the Jhelum for irrigation or building a barrage at Tulbul. “Our blood has been sucked and now the IWT has been cancelled.This should remain cancelled so that we can use this water properly,” Omar added.The IWT was signed between India and Pakistan in 1960. Under the treaty, India received full rights to use the waters of the three eastern rivers, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, while Pakistan received rights over the three western rivers, Indus, Chenab and Jhelum.India placed the treaty in abeyance last year following the Pahalgam terror attack. In May last year, after the treaty was placed in abeyance, Omar called for restarting the Tulbul Navigation Project on Wular Lake in north Kashmir. The project is located on Wular Lake in the Sopore area of Baramulla district. Pakistan has opposed construction of a 439-foot-long, 40-foot-wide barrage, also known as the Wular barrage or Tulbul Navigation Project, with a navigation lock on the lake.The Union govt began work on the project in 1984 to regulate water levels and facilitate navigation. However, work was halted a year later after Pakistan objected. Pakistan raised the issue with the Indus Waters Commission in 1986 and work was stopped in 1987.The governing National Conference in J&K has opposed the IWT all along, calling it detrimental to the interests of the people of Jammu and Kashmir.
Article Summary: India placed the treaty in abeyance last year following the Pahalgam terror attack. The IWT was signed between India and Pakistan in 1960. Under the treaty, India received full rights to use the waters of the three eastern rivers. Pakistan received rights over the three western rivers, Indus, Chenab and Jhelum.

Article Title: SC clears way for Tamil Nadu to give Karur victims’ kin jobs
Article Text:

Article Title: On Independence Day, TOI talks to Gandhi, Bose & Nehru
Article Text:
Jawaharlal Nehru (L) heads Tele-MANAS Centre of Telangana, CLN Gandhi retired from transport dept as addl commissioner

'Names bring history into an ordinary life'

In classrooms of generations past, an attendance register could sometimes sound like a roll call from India's freedom movement. Many parents named their children after national heroes. Today, those names are hard to find. But you can still come across a Gandhi, Nehru or Bose.Take Hyderabad's Jawaharlal Nehru . Born in the 1960s to freedom fighter and Congress member Mutteswara Rao, Nehru says his father was determined on the name of India's first PM. Rao reached out to him.The PMO pointed out Nehru was a surname and suggested the child be named Jawahar. But Rao was adamant."Being Jawaharlal Nehru, I feel, needs commitment," he says. He encouraged his only son to join the Army. "I stand for the country. I can proudly say my son is a Major."My father insisted he had a letter from Nehru giving his permission. That's how I became Jawaharlal Nehru," says the man who now heads Telangana govt's Tele-MANAS Centre. Nehru's sister, Vijayalakshmi Pandit, also has a modern-day namesake in Hyderabad. She was originally named Vijayalakshmi by her mother.Her father, a freedom fighter, later added Pandit to her name after the original became president of United Nations General Assembly.For Subhas Chandra Bose , a 33-year-old employee of Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences, the name came with expectations from childhood. "Everyone told me I should not do anything mediocre or bad because of my name," he says. "I still feel that responsibility. I don't even lie." His father didn't stop with one famous name.Subhas' brothers are named Chandrasekhar Azad and Ambedkar.There's also CLN Gandhi, a retired additional commissioner in the transport department, known simply as Gandhi in bureaucratic circles. "My father named me after Mahatma Gandhi as suggested by our neighbour, who was in the Army," he says. "I was always conscious of the values associated with my name."Socio-political analyst S Ramakrishna said: "When a child is named after a historical figure, that memory travels with the person. The name brings history into an ordinary life."
Article Summary: Hyderabad's Jawaharlal Nehru says his father was determined on the name of India's first PM. Nehru's sister, Vijayalakshmi Pandit, also has a modern-day namesake in Hyderabad. For Subhas Chandra Bose, the name came with expectations from childhood.

Around 2,500 cadets from the Army, Navy and Air Force, along with ‘My Bharat’ volunteers, participated in the celebrations, forming the words ‘Vande Mataram’ along Gyanpath.Around 5,000 special guests from different walks of life were invited to the ceremony, including women entrepreneurs, sanitation workers, street vendors, youth innovators, scientists, farmers, students and start-up founders. More than 1,500 people from different states and Union Territories also attended in traditional attire.Across the country, patriotic band performances were held at 343 prominent locations, while flag-hoisting ceremonies were also organised by the Indian Navy and local administrations in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep.
Article Summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio extended warm wishes to the people of India on the country's 80th Independence Day. Article Text:

JAMMU: A village defence guard (VDG) was killed Friday and another critically injured after a colleague allegedly opened fire following a brawl in J&K’s Udhampur, officials said.The fratricide unfolded in Damnote area Udhampur’s Panchari around 10am when Surjeet Singh turned the gun on his colleagues during the spat.“In a fit of anger, one of the VDGs fired on his colleagues. The shooting resulted in the death of VDG Baldev Singh and left Ramesh Singh injured,” an official said. He added that early preliminary probe indicated the attack arose out of personal enmity.Surjeet was arrested soon after, while Ramesh was rushed to Govt Medical College and Hospital in Udhampur town. “Further investigations are on,” the official said.VDGs are paid volunteers who work under police supervision in areas infested with militants or used by them as a corridor to enter the Kashmir Valley.

Jodhpur: In an embarrassing mix-up, Jodhpur zila parishad's chief executive officer, in his capacity as district election officer, Thursday issued a notice to Member of Parliament Manna Lal Rawat for negligence in election duties, mistakenly believing the latter still held a position as joint commissioner with the state transport department.The notice, which warned Rawat of potential disciplinary action due to a failure to update the list of his subordinate employees on the state govt's EMS (employee management system) portal in preparation for the upcoming municipal elections, was swiftly retracted following public ridicule on social media Friday.Rawat, who resigned from his state govt post prior to the 2024 general elections, is currently serving as a Lok Sabha member representing Udaipur on a BJP ticket. The goof-up occurred as a govt portal was not updated. Confirming this, Rawat said that district election officer (CEO, zila parishad) Ashish Kumar Mishra called him, admitted the mistake and withdrew the notice.Rawat was earlier posted as the transport department's joint commissioner in Jodhpur. He took voluntary retirement in 2024 to contest the parliamentary elections that year. Despite his retirement and subsequent election as a public representative, Rawat's name continued to figure in the list of govt employees maintained by the Jodhpur district election authorities.The error came to light after the notice was issued to him, raising questions over the way employee data is maintained and updated by the state election machinery. "It is surprising and worrisome," said Rawat, adding that despite the govt machinery operating in a digital environment, election-related data was still carrying information that was nearly three years old. Rawat questioned how govt departments were maintaining the data of ordinary citizens and serving employees if the records of a retired senior govt officer had not been removed from the list even after a considerable lapse of time.
Article Summary: Jodhpur zila parishad's chief executive officer issued a notice to Member of Parliament Manna Lal Rawat for negligence in election duties. He mistakenly believed the latter still held a position as joint commissioner with the state transport department. The notice was swiftly retracted following public ridicule on social media.

Article Title: 'Greatest threat': How India, Pakistan view each other; data lays bare deep animosity
Article Text:
A survey has revealed that a majority of adults in Pakistan and India view the other as their single greatest threat.

' Greatest threat ': India and Pakistan point at each other

The data paints a stark picture of two neighbours frozen in mutual distrust.

Mutual hostility runs deep

The numbers on bilateral perceptions are stark.

Lack of trust

When asked whether the Indian and Pakistani governments and people are committed to good relations with each other, the clear pattern is that people only have faith in their own country Pew Research report

Beneath the geopolitical differences lies a more fundamental problem: the absence of trust.

How Bangladesh, Sri Lanka view the rivals

The India-Pakistan divide extends beyond bilateral relations.

Divergent worldviews

Two countries, two very different worlds

Nearly eight decades after the 1947 Partition of British India gave birth to two independent nations, deep-seated historical trauma, and territorial disputes that have led to multiple military confrontations continue to shape the mindset of citizens on both sides of the border.As the two countries celebrate their independence, a major survey by the Pew Research Center reveals that an overwhelming majority of adults in both nuclear-armed rivals view the other as their single greatest geopolitical threat.Conducted across South Asia between February and May 2026, the findings highlight a persistent, deep-rooted mutual hostility that shows little sign of thawing. These sentiments reflect not merely political disagreements, but deeply entrenched unfavourable opinions among general populations, extending into perceptions of global superpowers, regional allies, and the long-term prospects for bilateral peace.The data paints a stark picture of two neighbours frozen in mutual distrust.In India, 54% of respondents named Pakistan as the greatest threat to their country.Conversely, 43% of Pakistanis identified India as their primary security threat.For Indians, China is the next most cited threat at 21%. For Pakistanis, Israel and the US each register at 24% as major threats — though still far below India.These threat perceptions align closely with how each public judges the other’s commitment to peace.Most Indians believe their own government and people are committed to good bilateral relations, but a majority say Pakistan’s government and people are not.Pakistanis mirror this: they express confidence in their own side’s commitment but doubt India’s.The numbers on bilateral perceptions are stark.Nearly nine in 10 Pakistanis have an unfavourable view of India, with 73% describing their opinion as 'very unfavourable'. The sentiment cuts across demographic groups, suggesting that hostility toward India is not confined to any particular section of Pakistani society.The picture in India is similarly bleak. As many as 78% of Indians have an unfavourable view of Pakistan, including 65% who hold a very unfavourable opinion. There is, however, a notable internal divide in India. Indian Muslims are somewhat more favorable toward Pakistan (21%) than Indian Hindus (6%), and they are also less likely to name Pakistan as their top threat (34% vs 57% among Hindus).Pew's polling also shows that this is not a temporary shift in sentiment.Indian views of Pakistan have remained overwhelmingly negative for more than a decade, with the share expressing a favourable opinion never rising above 20% since 2013.Historical Pew surveys also show that Pakistanis have long held predominantly negative views of India. Pakistani respondents expressing favourable views of India have generally ranged from single digits to around one-third.The survey further suggests that hostility is not simply about how Indians and Pakistanis perceive each other. It also extends to whether they believe the other side genuinely wants better relations.A clear pattern emerges: people tend to believe that their own government and population are committed to good bilateral relations, while doubting the intentions of the other side.A majority of Indians believe both the Indian government and Indian people are committed to maintaining good relations with Pakistan. But a majority of Pakistanis reject that assessment, saying the Indian government and people are not committed to good relations.The mirror image appears in Pakistan.A majority of Pakistanis say their government and people want good relations with India.Most Indians, however, believe Pakistan's government and people are not committed to improving ties. About a quarter of Indian respondents were unsure.This mutual lack of trust creates a difficult cycle: each side sees itself as willing to improve relations while viewing the other as unwilling to reciprocate.Indian Muslims again stand apart to some degree. Around a third say the Pakistani government and people are committed to good relations, significantly higher than the corresponding share among Indian Hindus.The Pew findings become even more revealing when India and Pakistan are placed alongside Bangladesh and Sri Lanka.Of the four South Asian countries surveyed, Sri Lanka is the only country that receives more positive than negative ratings from respondents in all three of the others.India, meanwhile, has the widest range of perceptions.Sri Lankans are overwhelmingly positive toward India, with 79% expressing a favourable opinion. In Bangladesh, 42% view India favourably. In Pakistan, however, the figure plunges to just 7%.India is also seen as Sri Lanka's most important ally by a clear majority: 63% of Sri Lankan respondents name India.The picture is very different in Bangladesh and Pakistan, where India is most often identified as the greatest threat.Views of Prime Minister Narendra Modi follow a broadly similar pattern. Seventy percent of Sri Lankans express confidence in PM Modi to do the right thing in world affairs, compared with 42% in Bangladesh and 4% in Pakistan.The survey also finds that Pakistan is not universally viewed negatively across South Asia.Fifty-seven percent of Sri Lankans and 54% of Bangladeshis have a favourable opinion of Pakistan, compared with only 8% of Indians.Bangladesh itself receives broadly positive views in Pakistan and Sri Lanka: 66% of Pakistanis and 56% of Sri Lankans express favourable opinions of Bangladesh. Only about a quarter of Indians do so.Sri Lanka emerges as the region's relative outlier. Around half or more of respondents in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh view the island nation positively, while significantly fewer hold negative views.The India-Pakistan divide extends beyond bilateral relations to the way each country views the global order.For Indians, Russia remains a particularly important and popular partner. Thirty-six percent identify Russia as India's most important ally, while 16% name the United States.Russia's favourable image in India is particularly striking. Fifty-eight percent of Indians have a favourable opinion of Russia, while 51% express confidence in Russian President Vladimir Putin.Pakistanis are considerably less positive: 39% have a favourable view of Russia and only 32% express confidence in Putin.India's relationship with the United States is also reflected in public opinion. Indians are substantially more favourable toward the US than Pakistanis are and are more likely to express confidence in US President Donald Trump.The picture is almost completely reversed when it comes to China.An overwhelming 90% of Pakistanis have a favourable view of China, while 83% express confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping. Three-quarters of Pakistanis identify China as their country's most important ally.Saudi Arabia is a distant second, named by 12%.In India, however, only around a quarter of respondents view China or Xi positively. Even Indian Muslims, who are more favourable toward China than Indian Hindus, remain negative toward both China and its president on balance.Nearly 80 years after Partition, the survey suggests that the India-Pakistan rivalry remains deeply embedded not only in government policy and military strategy, but also in public perceptions.The most striking finding may therefore not be that Indians and Pakistanis dislike each other. It is that both overwhelmingly believe the other side sees them as the problem.That mutual conviction — reinforced by decades of conflict, competing national narratives and geopolitical rivalry — remains one of the biggest barriers to changing the relationship between the two nuclear-armed neighbours.Yet beneath these geopolitical differences lies a more fundamental problem: the absence of trust.Both populations believe their own side is committed to better relations, while doubting the intentions of the other.
Article Summary: A majority of adults in both nuclear-armed rivals view the other as their single greatest geopolitical threat. In India, 54% of respondents named Pakistan as the greatest threat to their country. 43% of Pakistanis identified India as their primary security threat. For Indians, China is the next most cited threat at 21%.

Defence minister Rajnath Singh has hit back at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over his remarks on Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the government's foreign policy, calling them “petty and condemnable” and warning that such language could damage democratic discourse.Singh said he was particularly upset that the comments came from the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha. It is painful for me personally, too. In my long political life, I had never seen such indecent and unimaginable conduct from any LoP. Such conduct is a grave sign of a threat to a healthy democracy," Singh said.The defence minister also defended Modi's record as Prime Minister and his standing abroad, while arguing that political differences should not lead to what he described as disrespectful remarks."Rahul Gandhi might have frustration with PM in his mind, but such indecent remarks are unacceptable, especially when PM Modi has been a Prime Minister who has brought prestige to India nationally and internationally, and paved the way for Viksit Bharat. ""In 12 years, working with full dedication, he did not take any leave.Such indecent remarks against such a PM pain every Indian," he said.Singh then turned his criticism towards the Congress, questioning whether the party could continue to claim the legacy of several of India's prominent leaders after Gandhi's remarks."I would also like to humbly tell the Congress party that after such language and conduct, can they have any claim over the legacy of Lal-Bal-Pal and Gandhi, Patel and Nehru, from Subhas Babu to Rajendra Babu and Shastri ji and Narasimha Rao ji to Pranab Mukherjee?" Rajnath Singh said.He further accused Gandhi of not only targeting Modi but also damaging India's image and the dignity of the Leader of Opposition's office."With this conduct, Rahul Gandhi has not only insulted PM Narendra Modi but also the international prestige of India. He has shredded the dignity of the post of Lok Sabha LoP. I cannot even imagine that someone with the Gandhi surname can make such a shameful remark."The exchange followed remarks made by Gandhi at the Congress's Rachnatmak Congress National Convention in New Delhi on Thursday.Gandhi criticised the government's approach to foreign policy and argued that India's international relations should be driven by national interest rather than personal relationships between political leaders."I don't know where it came from; this idea got into their heads. I don't know who put it there or where it came from, the idea that foreign policy means hugging politicians. I was young. We went to America. Since we're talking about expressions, I'll share this. We went to America. I was twelve years old. Priyanka, myself, my mother, and my grandmother - my grandmother was the Prime Minister. There was a state dinner - an official dinner. My grandmother and mother went to the official dinner," he said.He added, "You aren't just visiting a friend's house. In this role, the Prime Minister of India doesn't engage in mere friendship. They have no interest in friendship; their job is to protect the country."Gandhi also accused the Modi government of damaging India's foreign policy, using the ongoing conflict involving Iran, the US and Israel as an example."War broke out in Iran. For India - had it recognised its own strength and had its leader been someone like Indira Gandhi--this presented the greatest opportunity in the world. What kind of opportunity? Iran was our old friend, America was our friend, and Russia was our friend. We could have stepped up, become relevant, and leveraged these friendships. But what actually happened? Nothing of the sort. Instead, Pakistan stepped in and took our place; Pakistan became the mediator, while India and Modi-ji simply looked on," he said.Rahul Gandhi claimed he receives "information directly from Modi ji's office these days; there is a full-blown revolt going on inside".He also referred to certain claims in videos on social media about China's actions concerning patrolling along the LAC in a border area of Arunachal Pradesh.He also raised allegations concerning Chinese activity along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Arunachal Pradesh and accused the government of pressuring the media not to report certain claims."In our patrolling areas--specifically in Arunachal--China blocked us from patrolling. They essentially said, 'Look, all that is fine--it is indeed your land--but you cannot patrol here.' Rajnath Singh, Amit Shah, and Narendra Modi have been completely deflated. They are calling up all the media editors, telling them, 'Don't publish this in your newspapers; suppress the story.' They are causing direct harm to the country without a second thought," he said.Gandhi also revisited the dispute over India's handling of the border situation with China following the Galwan clash.He alleged that conflicting statements about whether Indian territory had been lost weakened India's position during negotiations with China."After the Galwan incident, the Prime Minister held a meeting--a Zoom call. He stated that China hadn't taken a single inch of Indian territory. The Army said that our land had been taken. Just think about the message sent to China: Chinese negotiators asked our negotiators, 'What nonsense are you talking about? Your own Prime Minister said no land was lost.' So, internally, they have destroyed the country; they have wrecked our foreign policy. And they did all of this solely to finance their political structure, to secure funds from Adaniji," he alleged.
Article Summary: Defence minister Rajnath Singh has hit back at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over his remarks on Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the government's foreign policy. Singh said he was particularly upset that the comments came from the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha. He accused Gandhi of lowering the dignity associated with the post.

Article Title: Gandhi's letter to India, as told through TOI
Article Text:

Suspending Satyagraha

For Gandhi, non-violence was not merely tactical. Amid divisions within Congress and Subhas Chandra Bose’s different course, he wrote from Sevagram on July 21, 1941

The South Africa Years

Cow Slaughter And Eid

A fast unto death announced by Mahatma Gandhi in Pune’s Yerawada jail in 1932 was to change the course of India’s political history. Imprisoned for the Civil Disobedience Movement, Gandhi announced the fast in a Sept 13 letter to British PM Ramsay MacDonald that was shared with the press. His aim was to oppose a separate electorate for Dalits, proposed under the Communal Award of August 1932.“I have to resist your decision with my life,” Gandhi wrote, saying his fast would begin on Sept 20. “As a man of religion that I hold myself to be, I have no other course left open to me.”The award classified Dalits as a minority whose representatives would be elected only by Dalit voters, just as Muslims, Christians and Sikhs would elect their own representatives. Gandhi believed this would divide Hindu society; BR Ambedkar supported it as a safeguard for Dalit political representationGandhi acknowledged that he might be wrong. If his judgement was “warped”, he wrote, his death would be “a penance for my error” and would lift the burden from those who had “child-like faith” in his wisdom.His week-long fast led to the Poona Pact, negotiated by Madan Mohan Malaviya and Ambedkar and accepted by Gandhi. It abandoned a separate electorate but reserved seats for Dalits within the general electorate, becoming a milestone in Dalit representation and a precursor to reservations for SCs and STs in independent India.Gandhi also used a letter to the press to announce the suspension of Satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act.Writing on July 21, 1919, he asked satyagrahis to “swallow the bitter pill” and halt their campaign after protests had turned violent.The act allowed the colonial government to detain political prisoners for two years without trial. Gandhi’s campaign against it, launched in March 1919, was his first nationwide political mobilisation after returning from South Africa. Despite his appeals for peaceful hartals, fasts and prayers, violence erupted in several places. Gandhi was prevented from entering Punjab and arrested; the Jallianwala Bagh massacre on April 13 made the situation explosive. Attacks on police stations and railway property, and deadly clashes between protesters and authorities, led him to pause civil disobedience.In the July letter, published under the headline “SATYAGRAHA. Civil Resistance Suspended”, Gandhi disclosed that the governor of Bombay had conveyed “a grave warning” from the Government of India that renewed civil disobedience could threaten public security.Writing from Mani Bhavan in Bombay, Gandhi conceded that the suspension was painful. Yet he remained unyielding on the law: “Satyagrahi will pay for its removal with their lives if it cannot be removed by lesser means.” He also warned the Raj: “If my occasional Civil Resistance be a lighted match, Rowlatt legislation…is a thousand matches scattered throughout India.”For Gandhi, non-violence was not merely tactical. Amid divisions within Congress and Subhas Chandra Bose’s different course, he wrote from Sevagram on July 21, 1941: “With me, no doubt non-violence is an end in itself, though it is also a means for the attainment of the freedom of the country.” A year earlier, he had underlined its voluntary nature: “Non-violence cannot be imposed upon anyone. It has to come from within. ”Gandhi’s letters to the editor predated his emergence as a leader of India’s freedom struggle. During his 21 years in South Africa, where he first used Satyagraha as a method of resistance, he repeatedly drew attention to discriminatory laws against IndiansIn a Dec 19, 1901 letter, he described the restrictions in the Transvaal, where Indians could not hold land, were required to live and trade only in designated areas, and were barred from footpaths. In the Orange River Colony, he wrote, an Indian could not even enter without special permission, except as a domestic servant or labourer.After returning to India, he continued to write about the poor conditions of Indians legally settled in South Africa. In an Aug 29, 1919 letter, he blamed the “greedy Europeans of Natal” for importing Indian indentured labour at miserably low wages while ignoring local Zulu workers, all in pursuit of “enormous profits”.Gandhi’s correspondence also addressed social fractures, particularly Hindu-Muslim relations. In a 1919 letter written around Bakrid, he recounted a conversation with Maulana Abdul Bari of Lucknow’s Firangi Mahal, a prominent supporter of the Khilafat Movement.Gandhi quoted the Maulana as saying: “Islam will fall to pieces if it ever takes and never gives…. If we take from you, we must give to you.” Abdul Bari had urged his followers to abstain from cow slaughter. On Bakrid, he sent Gandhi a telegram: “In celebration of Hindu-Muslim unity, no cow sacrifices in Firangi-Mahal this Bakri-Id.”More than a century later, these letters are more than historical records. They reveal Gandhi not only as a politician confronting colonial power but as a public figure wrestling with representation, violence, communal division and moral responsibility. Through TOI’s pages, his words travelled beyond the immediate battles of the freedom struggle, leaving an intimate record of how he tried to shape public opinion — and India itself.
Article Summary: Gandhi’s campaign against the Rowlatt Act was his first nationwide political mobilisation after returning from South Africa. His week-long fast led to the Poona Pact, negotiated by Madan Mohan Malaviya and Ambedkar. It abandoned a separate electorate but reserved seats for Dalits.

NEW DELHI: The daughter of Karnataka BJP MLA B Suresh Gowda was booked for allegedly abusing and assaulting a woman police sub-inspector following an argument at a temple in Mandya district in Karnataka, police said on Friday.The incident took place on August 12 at the Maramma Temple in Ukkada village during Bhima Amavasya celebrations, news agency PTI reported.According to the complaint filed by the woman police officer, she was deployed at the temple for security duty when Aishwarya , the MLA's daughter, allegedly sought permission to enter the sanctum without waiting in the queue.The police officer alleged that she asked Aishwarya to wait to avoid inconvenience to other devotees. According to the complaint, Aishwarya then identified herself as the daughter of an MLA and questioned why she was being stopped.The argument allegedly escalated, with Aishwarya abusing the officer and hitting her on the head. The complainant also alleged that she was threatened and prevented from performing her official duties.Based on the complaint, the Kyathanahalli police registered an FIR under relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including charges related to assaulting a public servant, causing simple hurt, intentional insult and criminal intimidation, a senior police officer said.However, the case has taken another turn, with Aishwarya filing a counter-complaint against the police officer.Police said an inquiry into her allegations has been initiated, but no FIR has been registered on the basis of her complaint so far. Further action will depend on the findings of the inquiry.Speaking to reporters, Tumakuru Rural MLA B Suresh Gowda apologised for his daughter's conduct and said that anyone found guilty should face legal consequences."If she has committed a mistake, it is wrong. Whoever has done the mistake should face the consequences under the law," he said.The BJP legislator said his daughter had visited the temple with her two young children and had requested permission to enter briefly because waiting in the queue could have caused inconvenience.He also claimed that another person had been allowed to enter ahead of her, prompting his daughter to question the decision.While acknowledging that the argument had escalated, Gowda said his daughter should have shown greater restraint, particularly because she comes from a political family."I apologise on behalf of my daughter if she has made a mistake," he said.The MLA also called for a departmental inquiry into the incident and urged authorities to take action against anyone found responsible.
Article Summary: Karnataka BJP MLA B Suresh Gowda's daughter booked for allegedly abusing and assaulting a woman police sub-inspector. NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant has said that his oral remarks during a Supreme Court hearing were “misquoted” and later used with “malicious intent” to mislead the country’s youth, amid controversy over a comment that sparked the satirical online movement “Cockroach Janta Party”."My comment was misquoted and misused. All of us have rights and constitutional duty and responsibilities," he further said."When we speak of rights, we must also possess the capacity to fulfil our obligations. The over-a-month-long agitation culminated in a clash between protesters and police on July 20, leaving several people injured on both sides. Article Title: ‘Congress responsible for Partition’: CM Yogi says India would be different if Modi were PM in 1947
Article Text:
CM Yogi Adityanath said the Congress had failed the country by prioritising political power.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath has accused the Congress of being responsible for India's Partition and the violence that followed, arguing that the country's history could have been different under leaders such as Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel or Prime Minister Narendra Modi.Speaking at an event in Lucknow marking Partition Horrors Remembrance Day, CM Yogi said the Congress had failed the country by prioritising political power and alleged that the consequences of Partition continue to affect India.“Had Narendra Modi been the Prime Minister of India at the time of Independence, nobody would have been able to damage India in the slightest,” he was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.He also invoked Patel, saying that a leader of his stature would not have allowed India to be divided.“If a person like Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel were the Prime Minister at that time, nobody would have been able to disintegrate India ... The country had to pay a heavy price for the cowardice of these Congress members -- a character you all witnessed during the CAA protests,” he added.Adityanath alleged that areas including Sindh, Punjab and Bengal were handed over to Pakistan despite what he described as their Hindu and regional demographic character.“Bengal was Bengali-dominated. All Hindu villages were forcibly given to Bangladesh. This shameful act was committed by the Congress, which was extra-restless for power, and on whom the country had reposed its trust. It repaid that trust with betrayal,” he said.The chief minister also criticised the Congress over its response to attacks on Hindus in Bangladesh. He alleged that the party remained silent because it was concerned about losing electoral support.“They feared that reacting to the events in Bangladesh might cause their vote bank here to drift away. To them, the murder of Dalit Hindus holds no significance; what matters is their own vote bank,” he said.Adityanath further argued that internal divisions based on caste, region and language had historically weakened India and created opportunities for outside forces.“When such infighting exists, then conspiracy easily creeps in,” he said.He said the consequences of Partition could still be seen in the form of terrorism, Naxalism, Maoism and extremism. He also questioned the Congress's claims about its role in India's freedom struggle and accused the party of presenting itself as indispensable to the creation of modern India.“This also draws our attention to the silence we have all maintained regarding that pre-1947 conspiracy. Yet, even today, these people move before society, acting as if they were the ones who created India, and that without them, India would not have come into existence. It is a truly strange situation,” he said, describing Partition as the “darkest chapter of humanity.”Turning to what he described as the Congress's political legacy, Adityanath said institutions across the country had been named after one political family.“Every institution in the country came to bear the name of that very clan. Every single institution was named after that clan, and we all stood by silently, merely watching. What are they doing even today? What are their actions like now?” he said.The UP chief minister also defended the Citizenship Amendment Act and attacked the Congress's opposition to it.“There was no justification for opposing the act. The act contained a provision regarding Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Bangladesh -- territories that were once part of undivided India and share a heritage spanning thousands of years. It stipulated that if a Hindu, Sikh, Jain, Buddhist, Parsi, or Christian from these countries had been forced to leave and had sought refuge in India for five years, they would be granted Indian citizenship,” he said.He argued that the legislation did not provide for taking away land or property from Muslims or political parties, and accused opponents of using the issue to provoke protests.“Nowhere did it say that we would seize land belonging to Muslims, the Congress, or the Samajwadi Party. There was no such provision in the Act. Yet, attempts were made to incite agitation across the country,” he said.Adityanath also targeted the Samajwadi Party, claiming that Uttar Pradesh would have witnessed widespread unrest had it been in power during the CAA protests.“What kind of unbridled mayhem would have taken place? The rioters knew the price they would have to pay, which is why they could not act as they pleased; yet, their audacity was evident,” he said.“If you wish to see their true character, you would have witnessed it during the CAA protests, and their silence regarding the recent events in Bangladesh once again puts them in the dock,” Adityanath said.The event also featured a silent march led by Adityanath and other party leaders from the statue of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel to Lok Bhavan, according to the Uttar Pradesh government.
Article Summary: Yogi Adityanath said the Congress had failed the country by prioritising political power. He said the country's history could have been different under leaders such as Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel or Prime Minister Narendra Modi. He also criticised the Congress over its response to attacks on Hindus in Bangladesh.

NEW DELHI: Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian, amid the elevated tensions in West Asia, is set to visit New Delhi to attend the upcoming BRICS summit, Iranian sources told news agency ANI.Pezeshkian's participation in the summit is scheduled to be held in the national capital in September.The visit assumes significance as India is hosting the 18th BRICS Summit under its 2026 chairship. The summit will be held under India's theme of "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability". India assumed the BRICS chairship from Brazil at the beginning of 2026.Iran has signalled that it sees India as a potential partner in efforts to ease tensions in West Asia, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying New Delhi could play a greater role in de-escalating the ongoing crisis.Araghchi made the remarks during his visit to India in June for the BRICS foreign ministers' Meeting. Speaking to reporters in New Delhi, he said Tehran did not see a military solution to the conflict and believed that negotiations offered the only viable way forward.“We will welcome any constructive role by India,” Araghchi said, signalling Iran's openness to an Indian role in diplomatic efforts.His comments came as fighting and tensions continue to shape the security situation in West Asia following the outbreak of conflict on February 28 between Iran and the combined forces of the United States and Israel.India's relationship with Iran has also been marked by regular high-level engagement. In October 2024, Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian met Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia. The two leaders discussed bilateral ties as well as developments in the region.Iran became a full member of BRICS in 2024, joining Egypt, Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates as part of the group's expansion. Indonesia became a full member in 2025, taking the total number of members to 11.During his latest visit, Araghchi also met external affairs minister S Jaishankar to discuss regional developments and Iran's position on security around the Strait of Hormuz.Araghchi said Iran would continue to fulfil what he described as its historical responsibility for security in the strategically important waterway. He also sought to reassure countries that maintain friendly relations with Tehran about the safety of their commercial activity.“In fruitful engagement with my host external affairs minister S Jaishankar, discussed regional developments and clarified that Iran will always carry out historical duty as protector of security in Hormuz. Iran is a reliable partner of all friendly nations, who can rely on safety of commerce.”The Iranian government also highlighted Araghchi's intervention at the BRICS meeting, where he spoke about reducing Western dominance and preventing political considerations from influencing international institutions.“FM Seyyed Abbas Araghchi delivers Iran's statement at the BRICS foreign ministers' meeting in India. He highlighted the importance of breaking Western hegemony and ensuring that international institutions remain free from political manipulation.”The statements come at a time when West Asia remains caught in a fragile stalemate, with tensions continuing to simmer amid the wider conflict between Iran and the United States and Israel. For India, Tehran's invitation for a constructive role adds another dimension to its diplomatic engagement with both Iran and the wider region.

Iran has signalled that it sees India as a potential partner in efforts to ease tensions in West Asia.

Article Title: BCI action, U-turn and SC rebuke: How NALSAR students' protest against CJI kicked up a row
Article Text:
CJI Surya Kant rebukes BCI over NALSAR enrolment ban, says students have right to protest peacefully.

How the NALSAR row began

BCI threatens to block enrolment

BCI retracts order within hours

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Friday strongly disapproved of the Bar Council of India's now-revoked decision to stop enrolment of 2026 graduates of Hyderabad's NALSAR University of Law as advocates after students opposed his invitation as chief guest for the university's convocation. The Supreme Court said students had a right to protest peacefully and stayed any coercive action against NALSAR students or faculty by the BCI or state Bar Councils."If students are protesting peacefully, who is BCI to take action? It is the right of the students to protest peacefully. It is a dialogue between students and me. No one else has to step in," the CJI said.The bench, comprising CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, said the BCI's action was "absolutely uncalled for". The court posted the matter for hearing after two weeks.The controversy began after a section of NALSAR students urged the university to reconsider inviting CJI Kant as chief guest for its upcoming convocation. The students had cited his reported remarks during a hearing on alleged police excesses against protesters during the July 20 march to Parliament.At least six representations were submitted to the NALSAR administration from students of different batches, with the first being submitted on July 23.The students objected to the proposed invitation and referred to remarks attributed to the CJI during the hearing.One of the representations cited his response to an offer to show videos of the alleged police action: "We are not interested in videos; we don’t have time to watch." The letter also quoted him as telling counsel: "Don’t waste our time, and don’t waste your time".The students argued that inviting the CJI conflicted with the university's stated commitment to constitutional rights and access to justice."A convocation is meant to be a moment where the University’s own values, including a commitment to constitutional rights, access to justice, and reasoned engagement with grievances, are visibly reflected in the choices it makes. We feel that receiving our degrees from a dignitary whose recent public conduct, as reported, appears dismissive of serious allegations of police brutality against protesting citizens sits uncomfortably with what we have been taught to value during our time at NALSAR. "Five subsequent representations from different batches supported the concerns raised in the initial letter. Students claimed that hundreds had backed the representations, although the numbers could not be independently verified."We respect the CJI’s position. But we have been taught the Constitution and constitutional values, and we don’t want to support something that goes against those values," a student who was also part of the Student Bar Council told TOI.The issue escalated on Thursday when BCI chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra directed state Bar Councils not to enrol NALSAR's 2026 law graduates as advocates until further orders.The BCI sought a factual report from NALSAR on those who had allegedly initiated, organised or mobilised the campaign against CJI Kant's participation in the convocation.“Till further orders, no student of Nalsar University of Law, who has obtained law degree in the year 2026, shall be enrolled by any state bar council as an advocate.”Mishra said the final decision would be taken on August 19 after receiving a report from the university's vice-chancellor. He also asked NALSAR to distinguish between students who merely signed or supported representations and those who organised or coordinated the campaign or proposed an actual boycott.The BCI's initial letter also said, “A student of Law, having no regard or respect for the highest judicial office of the country, is not expected to be a responsible or sensible advocate, teacher or a judge. Such persons shall always be a liability on the profession. Such conduct reflects adversely upon the person’s suitability for entry into or association with the legal profession and is inconsistent with the dignity, discipline and ethical standards of the legal profession. ”The council further alleged that some academic staff had been involved in "misleading, instigating and misguiding" students.“As per some reliable sources, there exists groupism and dirty politics among some of the academic staff and they have played a very active role in misleading, instigating and misguiding the students. This is a very serious matter. The teachers, instead of involving themselves in their teaching job, are doing nasty politics in the campus. BCI, being the regulator of Legal Education cannot be a mute spectator of such a serious situation. ”The decision triggered criticism, including from Supreme Court Bar Association president Vikas Singh, who called the move arbitrary, illegal and disproportionate, although he said he did not support the students' opposition to the CJI's invitation.The BCI withdrew its initial directive later on Thursday following widespread criticism.In its revised communication, Mishra said the council had “thoroughly discussed and deliberated” on the earlier letter and modified its direction.He said the “vast majority” of NALSAR's 2026 graduating students were innocent and “were not inclined to take part in the move of disrespect”. However, he added that “It has been further reported by some reliable sources that a handful of teachers and outsiders were instrumental in instigating innocent students.”The BCI subsequently allowed the 2026 graduates to be enrolled while awaiting an inquiry report from NALSAR.On Friday, the Supreme Court's intervention effectively brought the focus back to the students' right to peacefully express their disagreement with the proposed convocation invitation.Kant said the matter represented a direct dialogue between the students and him, making clear that other institutions should not intervene in the students' peaceful protest.
Article Summary: CJI Surya Kant strongly disapproves of Bar Council of India's now-revoked decision to stop enrolment of 2026 graduates of Hyderabad's NALSAR University of Law as advocates. The Supreme Court said students had a right to protest peacefully and stayed any coercive action by the BCI or state Bar Councils.

NEW DELHI: The United Nations Security Council (UNSC) has officially attributed the November 2025 blast near Delhi’s iconic Red Fort to Al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS), according to the 38th report of its Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team.The attack on November 10 last year claimed 11 lives."Al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS, not listed) continued to evolve from a fragmented group into a regional terrorist entity; it established logistics and financial networks, working in decentralised, small, scattered cells instead of large units. The attack in November 2025 on the Red Fort in Delhi was officially attributed to AQIS," the report, published on August 10, stated.The assessment marks a significant shift in the attribution of the Red Fort attack, which had earlier been linked to the Pakistan-based Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM).The report noted that one member state had attributed a series of attacks to JeM and also linked the group to the Red Fort blast.The explosion occurred around 7 pm when a moving Hyundai i20 erupted in flames near the iconic monument.Investigators identified Umar-e-Nabi as the driver of the car and suspect him of carrying out the attack as a suicide bomber.Read also: Red Fort blast: 7,500-page NIA charge sheet alleges ‘Operation Heavenly Hind’ to overthrow govt Launched in 2014, AQIS is a regional affiliate of Al-Qaida.The group was formed to expand the organisation’s activities across South Asia, including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and parts of Afghanistan.Meanwhile, the latest UNSC assessment also flagged broader concerns over the activities and capabilities of Al-Qaida and Islamic State (ISIL/Da’esh) affiliates.The report noted that Al-Qaida and ISIL had for years shown interest in developing chemical and biological weapons but had so far failed to overcome the technical challenges involved. It also highlighted the widespread circulation of instructions on producing such agents in online terrorist communities.The report cited material published by ISIL’s English-language Invade magazine in February that included instructions related to botulinum toxin and cyanide. It also noted that ISIL-K had shown particular interest in ricin and circulated instructions on developing the toxin over the previous 12 months.
Article Summary: The United Nations Security Council has officially attributed the November 2025 blast near Delhi’s iconic Red Fort to Al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent (AQIS) The assessment marks a significant shift in the attribution of the Red Fort attack, which had earlier been linked to the Pakistan-based Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM)

Article Title: Nigel Farage beats ‘space warrior trashcan’ rival in UK bypoll he triggered
Article Text:
Nigel Farage, Leader of Britain's Reform UK party stood against 'Count Binface' to fight for a seat as MP in UK

Why was the by-election held?

Who is Count Binface?

Why the by-elections?

Nigel Farage secured a confortable victory in the UK parliamentary by-election. However, the biggest challenge emerged was a self-proclaimed intergalactic space warrior dressed as a trash can, in a contest that was boycotted by all major Westminster parties.Farage, leader of Reform UK, secured 22,239 votes, or 63.3 per cent, to retain his Clacton seat. His closest challenger was Count Binface, the satirical persona of comedian Jonathan Harvey, who received 9,455 votes, or 26.9 per cent.Farage became Clacton's MP at the 2024 general election but resigned from Parliament in July amid scrutiny over his financial affairs. The resignation triggered a by-election, which Farage then contested to win back his seat.Farage had said he wanted the people of Clacton to judge him over the allegations, framing the election as a contest between voters and the political establishment.Labour, the Conservatives, Liberal Democrats, Greens and Restore Britain all declined to field candidates, calling the election a political stunt or gimmick.The absence of the major parties left Farage facing 33 other candidates, many of them independents or novelty candidates.Only Farage and Count Binface retained their £500 deposits after the vote.Count Binface is the satirical character played by British comedian Jonathan Harvey. He campaigned in a distinctive bin-shaped helmet, describing himself as an intergalactic space warrior.His manifesto was built around political satire and deliberately absurd proposals. In Clacton, he promised to nationalise singer Adele, "cut your taxes, and raise everyone else's" and impose a windfall tax on celebrity crime novels.Despite the jokes, Binface secured 26.9% of the vote, or more than one in four votes cast. It was a strong performance for a novelty candidate.After the result, Binface joked that he had won among the candidates who had "bothered to turn up", referring to Farage's absence from the count.The by-polls were triggered because Farage resigned after facing scrutiny over a £5 million gift from Reform UK donor Christopher Harborne. A parliamentary standards investigation had been examining whether he failed to declare the gift.Farage has denied wrongdoing and argued that resigning and seeking re-election would allow voters to deliver their verdict.The investigation was paused after he resigned but has now resumed following his victory, reported BBC.If the standards commissioner finds that Farage breached parliamentary rules, he could face sanctions, including suspension from the House of Commons. The process could ultimately trigger another by-election in Clacton.Farage did not attend the declaration of the result, saying police had warned him about an alleged campaign to disrupt the event. He later told supporters he was "damned if" he would stand on a stage after a "resounding victory" only to be "demeaned and humiliated by nobodies".Essex Police said there had been no incidents or issues and that attending the count was a decision for individual candidates and their security teams.The by-election, contested by a record 34 candidates, is estimated to have cost taxpayers about £250,000.
Article Summary: Farage secured 22,239 votes, or 63.3 per cent, to retain his Clacton seat. His closest challenger was Count Binface, the satirical persona of comedian Jonathan Harvey, who received 9,455 votes. The by-election, contested by a record 34 candidates, is estimated to have cost taxpayers £250,000.

Article Title: ‘First Islamic republic with nuclear weapons’: Netanyahu lashes out at UK
Article Text:
Netanyahu’s comments came as he also pushed back against a US-backed plan aimed at ending the Gaza war

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has launched a sharp rebuke against the UK, calling it the “Islamic republic of Britain” and describing it as a potential “first Islamic republic with nuclear weapons” in a podcast interview.Netanyahu made the comments during a podcast interview for Israel’s Army Radio, while discussing what he sees as a shift in British attitudes towards Israel. He praised the positive coverage Israel received from journalist Randolph Churchill, the son of former British prime minister Winston Churchill, more than half a century ago, before contrasting it with what he described as the situation in Britain today.“Go find that in today’s Britain, in what is called the Islamic republic of Britain,” Netanyahu said.When the host questioned whether Netanyahu was unfairly singling out the UK and asked, “Isn’t all of Europe is like that?”, the Israeli prime minister doubled down.“Yes, but you know someone said the first Islamic republic with nuclear weapons will be the Islamic republic of Britain.”His comments come amid increasingly strained relations between Britain and Israel, particularly over the war in Gaza. Shortly before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham apologised for Labour’s initial response to Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, saying the party “didn’t get it right” and needed to “do better” under his leadership.Netanyahu’s comments came as he also pushed back against a US-backed plan aimed at ending the Gaza war, signalling continued disagreement with Washington over the terms of any deal involving Hamas.He said Israel would not withdraw from its current positions in Gaza until Hamas was completely disarmed. The proposed agreement called for Hamas to begin disarming while Israel halted its strikes and withdrew from roughly 60% of the territory it currently controls.“The Trump administration “sent us a draft. We did not agree. It is not our draft. We sent our comments. … This is our position,” Netanyahu said in a video posted on social media.He also said Israeli forces would continue to “do whatever is necessary to protect themselves, our territory, and our citizens.”The comments came as Palestinians held a mass funeral for more than 100 bodies recovered from a residential block in Gaza City’s Sabra neighbourhood that was destroyed in an Israeli strike in November 2023.The recovery of the remains has been possible during the fragile ceasefire, with rescue workers retrieving the bodies of 112 people, including 40 children, from the rubble. Gaza’s Civil Defense said 157 bodies from the site remain missing.
Article Summary: Netanyahu made the comments during a podcast interview for Israel’s Army Radio. He was discussing what he sees as a shift in British attitudes towards Israel. His comments come amid increasingly strained relations between Britain and Israel. He also pushed back against a US-backed plan aimed at ending the Gaza war.

Article Title: Second train derails in Southeast England within 24 hours; no injuries reported
Article Text:
Second train derailed in UK, no injuries reported/Image: X

Second derailment in less than a day

A second train has derailed in southeast England in less than 24 hours, with rear carriages coming off the tracks near Wickford in Essex.The incident happened shortly after 2pm local time on Friday, according to British Transport Police. The force said the rear carriages remained upright after derailing.Emergency services, including police, paramedics and firefighters, were sent to the scene. No injuries have been reported.The cause of the derailment was not immediately known.The Essex incident comes less than 24 hours after a passenger train derailed near Lewes in East Sussex on Thursday afternoon.The Southern service came off the tracks shortly before 4pm BST, with at least two carriages reportedly overturning. Eighteen people were injured, including two seriously, according to reports.Emergency crews attended the scene near Lewes station, while the disruption affected services between Haywards Heath and Lewes. The cause of that derailment has not yet been established.
Article Summary: Second train derailment in less than a day in southeast England. Rear carriages came off tracks near Wickford, Essex, on Friday. No injuries have been reported. Comes less than 24 hours after a train derailed near Lewes, East Sussex. Eighteen people were injured, including two seriously.

Article Title: Pakistani minister in Balochistan province escapes armed attack on convoy
Article Text:
All six injured people suffered bullet wounds, according to a senior police official.​

Balochistan home minister Mir Ziaullah Langove escaped unharmed after armed attackers targeted his convoy in Mastung district on Friday, injuring six people, including three police personnel.The attack took place in the Khad Kocha area as Langove was travelling from Quetta to Kalat, Balochistan government spokesperson Shahid Rind said."Six people were injured in the attack, but the minister remained unhurt and the convoy has returned to Quetta," Rind said.All six injured people suffered bullet wounds, according to a senior police official. Three of them were police personnel, with two reportedly in serious condition. They were taken to a hospital in Quetta for treatment.The attack has raised fresh security concerns in Khad Kocha, an area that has repeatedly come under attack in recent weeks.According to officials, this was the fourth attack on travellers along the same highway since last month. Insurgents have repeatedly targeted people travelling through the area despite a major security operation carried out following the earlier incidents.Security forces have now sealed off the area and launched a search operation to locate those responsible for the latest attack.The incident adds to the continuing security challenges in Balochistan, where armed insurgent groups have carried out attacks against security forces and civilians.
Article Summary: Balochistan home minister Mir Ziaullah Langove escaped unharmed after armed attackers targeted his convoy. The attack took place in the Khad Kocha area as Langove was travelling from Quetta to Kalat. All six injured people suffered bullet wounds, according to a senior police official.

Article Title: Volhynia massacres: Russia using WWII to plant discord between Ukraine and Poland?
Article Text:
Polish officials and researchers say Moscow has sharply increased online messaging around the Volhynia massacres.

How Russia is 'exploiting' the Volhynia dispute

The facts may be real, but the narrative can still be manipulated

Ukraine fatigue creates fertile ground for the campaign

Russia is being accused of using a painful chapter in the history of Poland and Ukraine to deepen tensions between the two countries, as Warsaw and Kyiv remain divided over the killings that took place during World War 2.Polish officials and researchers say Moscow has sharply increased online messaging in Poland around the Volhynia massacres, while also using the issue to fuel anger against Ukrainians living in the country.The campaign has largely played out on social media, with much of the content appearing in Polish. Analysts say the aim is not always to create completely false stories, but to amplify real disputes in ways that can deepen existing divisions.The historical dispute centres on the Volhynia massacres between 1943 and 1945. Poland says Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Poles during the violence, while thousands of Ukrainians were also killed in retaliatory attacks.Tensions over the issue increased after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy named an army unit after insurgents linked to the massacres. Polish president Karol Nawrocki, who is from the political right, responded by stripping Zelenskyy of a major Polish honour in June.Polish deputy digital minister Pawel Olszewski said the disagreement was quickly followed by a surge in Russian messaging across social media and Russian media platforms, including Telegram.Research by the state-backed Polish Institute of International Affairs found that Polish-language anti-Ukrainian content on X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube rose by more than 250% after Zelenskyy's decision.Filip Bryjka of PISM said much of this increase appeared to have been artificially boosted through bots, creating the impression that anti-Ukrainian sentiment was spreading rapidly.Analysts say one reason this type of campaign is difficult to detect is that it does not necessarily depend on completely fabricated information.Instead, genuine events and historical grievances can be repeatedly highlighted and framed in ways that encourage anger towards a particular group."The event is real, but the interpretation is imposed by an external actor," said Wojciech Pokora, an analyst at Info Ops Poland Foundation.Moscow has rejected the accusations. The Russian embassy in Warsaw said Russia does not interfere in relations between other countries."The Russian Federation does not interfere in the relations between other states," the Russian embassy in Warsaw said in an emailed statement, adding that accusations about Russia spreading disinformation to undermine support for Ukraine are baseless.The issue has gained greater importance because Poland remains one of Ukraine's strongest supporters in its war against Russia, but public backing for Ukraine has weakened.An IBRiS poll published last month found that 33.6% of respondents said their attitude towards Ukrainians had worsened following the latest dispute linked to the World War Two killings.Another IBRiS survey found that support for continuing military assistance to Ukraine had fallen to 52%, compared with 78% in 2022.Researchers caution that declining support for Ukraine cannot be blamed entirely on Russian influence.Poland is home to an estimated 1.8 to 1.9 million Ukrainian migrants, while disagreements over grain imports and the unresolved legacy of the Volhynia killings have also contributed to public frustration.Olszewski said the Russian messaging had "fallen on fertile ground".Meanwhile, hostility towards Ukrainians in Poland has reportedly increased, prompting prime minister Donald Tusk to call for an end to xenophobic attacks.The issue could become even more politically significant ahead of Poland's 2027 parliamentary elections. Polling suggests Tusk's pro-European government could struggle to retain power, while support for the far-right has been growing.That makes the Volhynia dispute more than a historical argument. For Poland, it touches on a painful national memory. For Ukraine, it is part of a complicated shared history with its neighbour. And for Russia, Polish analysts argue, the disagreement offers an opportunity to deepen divisions between two countries that have otherwise stood together against Moscow.
Article Summary: Polish officials and researchers say Moscow has sharply increased online messaging around the Volhynia massacres. Campaign has largely played out on social media, with much of the content appearing in Polish. Analysts say aim is not always to create completely false stories, but to amplify real disputes in ways that can deepen existing divisions.

Article Title: Zeeshan Siddique gets death threat from Portugal number, caller claims Godara gang link
Article Text:
NCP leader Zeeshan Siddique reported receiving a death threat from a Portugal-based number (File photo)





MUMBAI: National Congress Party leader and MLC Zeeshan Siddique filed a complaint soon after he arrived in Mumbai on Friday morning after a fresh threat he received while he was in London at 2.36 (which was 7.06 am IST).Bandra police registered a non-cognisable (NC) offence against an unknown person based on an audio threat he received on August 12.Siddique received the threat audio clip from a Portugal number.Siddique confirmed TOI that Bandra police registered an NC based on the complaint he submitted."The audio threat that lasted 1.29 minutes was received on my WhatsApp number by the same person who identified himself as Zeeshan Akhtar. My sister filed the first NC on August 6 while I was abroad. Now, the death threat audio clip was sent directly to me using Portugal number. In November 2025, we filed the writ and soon my security cover was reduced from eight cops to two. Also, there was 22 cops deployed at my residence which was reduced to zero," he said.The person who sent the audio threat dared Siddique to go and file a police complaint himself instead of sending his sister forward to file the complaint and threatened he will the one to kill him.TOI extracts the transcript of the threat audio which states, "Listen here, Zeeshan Siddique, this is Zeeshan Akhtar speaking. Listen to me carefully: I am going to kill you. Before I even touch your father... well, I had already assigned a team to the task two years ago, back when I was in police custody, got it?""Brother, everyone I’ve killed, I did so openly. Now, your end has come. Don't push your sister to the forefront; if you have the guts, go file the complaint yourself. I know everything; I’m aware of every detail. You might not die today or tomorrow, but within a year, you will definitely die. I have no problem with your money and I am not threatening you for money. The person claimed that he object to my illegal business and for which he will kill me. He threatened: 'You will die, and I am the one who will kill you'," the transcript stated further.The first threat compaint was filed by Siddique's sister Arshia on August 6. She was in the Bombay High Court (HC) for the hearing of a writ petition filed for initiating action against a builder whose role is suspected behind their father's murder."This is not coincidence. Both the threats are being made when the dates for the writ petition was nearing," he said.DCP (West Zone-2) Mohit Garg confirmed about the fresh NC registered on complaint from Siddique.A case of criminal intimidation involving severe threats, such as threatening death and grievous hurt was registered against unknown person.
Article Summary: Siddique received the threat audio clip from a Portugal-based number. Bandra police registered a non-cognisable (NC) offence against an unknown person. The person who sent the audio threat dared Siddique to go and file a police complaint himself instead of sending his sister forward to file the complaint.

Article Title: ‘We can drive them crazy’: Rahul Gandhi takes aim at PM Modi, Amit Shah
Article Text:
Rahul addressed a conclave of Rachnatmak Congress
